items.title: ‘They’re Demonic’: Astronaut Who Walked on the Moon on Shocking Truth About Aliens
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "That's ... what God showed me."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former astronaut Charlie Duke is known for being the youngest man to walk on the moon. But Duke, 91, is also a strong Christian who has a fascinating perspective on aliens and UFOs, subjects that have received a plethora of attention of late.

The astronaut, who was the spacecraft communicator for the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969 and spent 265 hours in space during that time, told CBN News he once wasn’t so sure about his beliefs on the true nature of aliens and UFOs.

“For a long time [years ago] I was praying about UFOs, and asked for a sign,” Duke said. “I felt like UFOs were demonic … but I was saying that at rotary clubs and stuff like that, and people were laughing me off the stage.”

So, he asked the Lord to help him come to a definitive conclusion that would settle the matter once and for all.

“I said, ‘God, if I’m really right about this, then give me a sign tomorrow morning that a very good friend of mine at breakfast will start talking about UFOs,'” he said. “And this guy’s a businessman. He never talks about science stuff or … stuff like that. So the next morning at breakfast, we sat down, he said, ‘Charlie, come on over. I wanna start talking to you about UFOs.'”

Duke interpreted this as an answer to his prayer. The former astronaut then appealed to Scripture to make his case, looking at the Bible’s description of Satan to further conclude his position.

“The Lord says what we’re seeing is real, but the devil can appear as an angel of light, the Bible says,” he said. “And so what I believe … is the UFOs are trying to turn us away from the truth and run after these alien beings, which are really not beings at all. They’re demonic.”

Ultimately, Duke said he’s unconcerned with those who might laugh at him or mock his perspective on the matter.

“You can laugh at me if you want to, but that’s … what God showed me, and I’m sticking to it,” he said.

Duke said he never personally viewed anything on his flight to the moon that would be considered alien or UFO-like. Watch the interview above for more.

items.title: Actress Evangeline Lilly Flees Hollywood: ‘God Has a Plan’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "So intense."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Actress Evangeline Lilly has had a sweeping Hollywood career, playing beloved characters in TV shows like “Lost” and films like “The Hobbit.”

But despite a wildly popular career, Lilly decided back in 2020 to step back from Hollywood — a decision that sparked quite a bit of media interest.

“It’s been six years now,” she said, noting the media caught on to the story after she posted a retrospective in 2024. “When I was 26, I was saying … all the things I wanted in my life … and I did it … I’m there,” she said. “I’ve already retired [by 2024 when the retrospective came out]. At that point, I’ve been retired for four years … it’s been a long time of adjusting.”

Lilly said she had no idea what the “consequences” of her decision might be, though she described moments of fear as she “let go of so much … power, influence, and potential money.” There was also the affirmation piece of the puzzle.

“When you’re successful at something, it feels really good when the world says, ‘We love you! You’re amazing!’ Like, this is a wonderful feeling,” Lilly said. “How do you walk away from that? And I’ve had moments of … gripping fear of like, ‘What am I doing?’ But, ultimately, the decision was one that was made in great conviction.

Before becoming an actress, Lilly studied political science and international relations and wanted to become a missionary, humanitarian, or diplomat.

“I wanted to make the world a better place,” she said. “And there are many people who will claim that actors are making the world a better place, that they’ve had an impact on their lives. But…I’ve always wanted a much more hands-on impact. I’ve done 22 years of hands-on humanitarian work in Rwanda.”

But Lilly said she wants to do more and wants to help people heal and find wholeness.

“I love telling stories, but I’d like to tell stories of my own instead of being in front of the camera,” she said. “I’d much prefer a quieter position. I’ve always hated being famous. I never made any secrets about that. I’ve always said being famous is the cost of the wealth that you can get as an actor. Like that’s what you pay for — the wealth.”

Now, she feels liberated and said she has stepped into a “total trust and surrender that God has a plan for my life.”

Despite mostly stepping out of Hollywood, Lilly is now lending her voice to a different type of project: “Legend of Destruction,” a film that tells the “story of the Jewish revolt against Rome, which ended with the destruction of the Temple in the year 70.”

“The film was originally made in Hebrew, and so I actually was able to see the fully completed piece before I came on board for the English version,” she told CBN News. “I didn’t understand what I was looking at. I didn’t understand what I was being invited into, but I watched the film, and within the first…three to four seconds of the film, I felt like I was just completely immersed in a way that most films don’t do for me anymore.”

What makes “Legend of Destruction” unique is that it’s made of still paintings, with Lilly, who portrays Queen Bernice, and other actors using their voices to dramatically retell the story.

“This story was so intense and beautifully told, and then also incredibly timely because it’s talking about a society divided unto itself,” Lilly said. “So a society that’s really broken and in civil strife and how that leads ultimately to mutual destruction amongst all of its people.”

Given that the film deals with the destruction of the Second Temple, many people will be interested in this unique film.

“At that time, Jerusalem was under threat from the Roman Empire. The Romans were coming to destroy the temple and to take over the city,” Lilly said. “The outcome of that could have potentially been different had the Israeli people been unified, but they were so disenchanted, they were so disenfranchised from one another, they were so divided that they were actually killing each other before the Romans ever even got a chance to arrive. It’s an incredible story. That’s what drew me in.”

The “Lost” star said the events in “Legend of Destruction” take place about 33 years after Christ’s death, meaning they are very much part of the world Jesus was born into.

items.title: It Costs the Average American an Hour of Work to Buy 10 Staple Groceries. In Some Countries, It Takes More Than 19 Days
items.author: Hannah Lee
items.summary: Ten basic foods now cost more than a week of work in 11 of the 56 countries surveyed in a new Price Shocks report from World Vision, and nine of those 11 are in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Sudan, buying them takes 19.3 eight-hour workdays. In Myanmar, 10.1, and in Haiti, 9.5. In the Central African&#8230
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Ten basic foods now cost more than a week of work in 11 of the 56 countries surveyed in a new Price Shocks report from World Vision, and nine of those 11 are in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Sudan, buying them takes 19.3 eight-hour workdays. In Myanmar, 10.1, and in Haiti, 9.5. In the Central African Republic, buying them takes 30.1 days. In the U.S., it takes an hour.

Between November 2025 and May 2026, researchers priced the same ten foods at local markets, shops and supermarkets: a kilogram each of bananas, rice, wheat flour, sugar, maize and tomatoes, a dozen eggs, a liter of cooking oil, a liter of milk and one raw chicken. They then compared the cost of those ten foods with each country’s average income per person, adjusted for purchasing power, to work out how many hours of work it takes to afford them. That is a national average, not a minimum wage, so a lower-paid worker would need even longer.

Average income can hide inequality and may overstate what the poorest families can buy. Four countries with active conflict or collapsed institutions, South Sudan, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela, were left out of the hours analysis because there was no income data to compare, so the survey found bad situations but misses the worst ones.

Sudan shows how hard a conflict zone is to measure. The survey recorded the Sudanese price of the ten foods getting 36 percent cheaper than in 2024, yet the report says famine was present in parts of the country in 2025 and 2026, and Sudan is still one of the least affordable places in the study.

The report also profiles families living with the numbers.

Khin, 45, earns money ironing and washing clothes in Myanmar’s Yangon Region. Her husband can’t work because of poor health, and they have eight children. “There are days when my children eat rice with only oil and salt,” she is quoted as saying. “This is no longer occasional; it has become a daily reality.”

She says her twins are becoming malnourished and having digestive issues. Her 12-year-old daughter, Chit, told the report’s authors that fish and chicken have given way to spinach, tea leaf salad and fermented fish sauce.

In Hinche, Haiti, Cherlande runs a market stall that pays for her children’s school, their clothes and the family’s food, and she says she has no other income. A cup of rice that cost 20 or 25 gourdes now costs 50, she says, and a small packet of spaghetti has gone from 50 gourdes to 100. “You can’t afford to eat meat every day,” she said.

In 2025, an estimated 35.5 million children were acutely malnourished worldwide, nearly 10 million of them severely, according to the Global Report on Food Crises figures the report cites. Malnutrition can damage a child’s physical and cognitive development and weaken immunity, and the effects can last into adulthood.

The report asks governments, donors and businesses to protect children’s access to food during crises, expand school meals and social protection, and invest in local food systems. Compassion International works on the same problem from another angle, and says it provides children living in poverty with care that includes meals, tutoring and medical care.

TAKE ACTION

Read the full report, pass it to someone who has never thought about groceries in terms of days of work, and pray for the families behind the numbers.

items.title: With All Your Heart, Soul, and Mind
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel this Sunday is from the twenty-second chapter of the Gospel of Matthew.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel this Sunday is from the twenty-second chapter of the Gospel of Matthew. Jesus has been doing battle with the scribes and Pharisees, and this passage brings that great argument to a conclusion in an interesting way. One of the teachers of the law, making an old move in rabbinic circles, tests him: “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” In other words, can you sum up the richness and complexity of the law in one statement? When Jesus gives his answer, we’re on holy ground, because this is not just one rabbi among many but the Lord—the Word made flesh—telling us what’s at the very heart of the matter.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Exodus 22:20-26

Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the Lord alone, shall be devoted to destruction.

You shall not wrong or oppress a resident alien, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt. You shall not abuse any widow or orphan. If you do abuse them, when they cry out to me, I will surely heed their cry; my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children orphans.

If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you, you shall not deal with them as a creditor; you shall not exact interest from them. If you take your neighbor’s cloak in pawn, you shall restore it before the sun goes down;

Psalm
Psalm 18:2-3, 3-4, 47, 51

The Lord is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer,
    my God, my rock in whom I take refuge,
    my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.
I call upon the Lord, who is worthy to be praised,
    so I shall be saved from my enemies.
I call upon the Lord, who is worthy to be praised,
    so I shall be saved from my enemies.
The cords of death encompassed me;
    the torrents of perdition assailed me;
the God who gave me vengeance
    and subdued peoples under me;

Second Reading
1 Thessalonians 1:5c-10

 because our message of the gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction; just as you know what kind of persons we proved to be among you for your sake. And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for in spite of persecution you received the word with joy inspired by the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia. For the word of the Lord has sounded forth from you not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith in God has become known, so that we have no need to speak about it. For the people of those regions report about us what kind of welcome we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who rescues us from the wrath that is coming.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 22:34-40

When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together, and one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.”

items.title: The Culture of Death is on the Ballot This November
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

The pro-life movement has its work cut out for it. In 2026, four state abortion initiatives are on the ballot in Nevada, Virginia, Idaho, and Missouri.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

On the eve of November elections, surveys indicate Americans’ economic concerns, including the cost of groceries, gas, and other living expenses, will predominate when they go to the polls. Yet nearly half of American voters say that abortion will be a “very important” issue to them come election day. And indeed, abortion is on the ballot in a handful of states that could determine the fate of thousands of babies in the coming years.

Since 2022, eleven states have established state constitutional rights to abortion: California, Michigan, Vermont, Arizona, Colorado, Maryland, Missouri, Montana, New York, Ohio, and Nevada. Meanwhile, in only three states were pro-abortion pushes to amend the constitution defeated: Florida, Nebraska, and South Dakota. A few other states have considered initiatives related to whether their constitutions should be interpreted to protect the right to abortion. Overall, the pro-abortion win rate in the post-Dobbs era has been 78.5 percent, with several wins in “purple” and “red” states. Money is a factor: In 2024 alone, pro-abortion forces outspent pro-life forces six to one. Clearly, in a post-Roe world, the pro-life movement has its work cut out for it. In 2026, four more state abortion initiatives are on the ballot in Nevada, Virginia, Idaho, and Missouri.

In Nevada, abortion is currently lawful up to twenty-four weeks. If Question 6 were approved, Nevada would embrace abortion extremism. It would establish abortion as a fundamental right that can only be limited by a “compelling state interest,” which is defined narrowly to include only the mother’s life or health. The language mentions fetal viability, but this is a mere fig leaf, since the abortion right can be asserted after viability if the “life or health” of the mother is at stake, which can include “psychological” health (a fuzzy idea that harkens back to Roe v. Wade’s companion case, Doe v. Bolton, which is broad enough to encompass emotional distress). In short, if this constitutional amendment is passed, Nevada would join the Wild West of the most extreme pro-choice States where abortion-on-demand is entrenched as a fundamental right. 

In Virginia, voters will similarly have to decide for or against abortion extremism in Question 1, the “Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment.” The pro-abortion framing of this initiative is notable for its peculiar “mixture of vagueness and sheer incompetence,” which George Orwell observed had become characteristic of English political writing by the mid-twentieth century. No one contests the negative right of adults to reproduce, unmolested by the state. At the moment of conception, reproduction has occurred, and therefore, the right to reproduce is protected everywhere in America, since all states permit freely consenting adults to conceive or not to conceive. In a bit broader sense, reproductive freedom could also include, as Question 1 does, the right to determine one’s “prenatal care” and “postpartum care.” But Question 1 absurdly lumps these rights in with “abortion care.” Abortion, the intentional killing of an unborn child as an end or a means is never “care.” Nor is it an aspect of “reproductive freedom,” which in the overwhelming majority of cases was already exercised (excepting, e.g., conception by rape). No matter the circumstances of conception, it is always and everywhere a harm that destroys a human life.

Idaho’s Proposition 1 is a bit different. It is a citizen-initiated ballot measure (they had to collect about 70,000 signatures), which would establish a more qualified right to abortion than in Nevada and Virginia in that it would permit abortions after fetal viability only in “medical emergencies.” This is a more restrictive standard since presumably a sixteen-year-old girl anxious about fitting into her prom dress would not constitute a medical emergency. Yet like Virginia and Nevada, Proposition 1’s right to “reproductive freedom” is guaranteed to every person, which includes minors, and therefore extends a right to minors to get abortions without parental consent. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

This is one of the more insidious features of the militant pro-abortion measures of 2026. They strike at the heart of the family not only through the nascent maternal bond of pregnant young women, but at the cords of love and honor that bind them to their parents. 

Finally, Missourians will consider whether to repeal Amendment 3, in which voters very narrowly established a constitutional right to abortion in 2024. Since then, all manner of restrictions on abortion have been struck down, including modest restrictions that had been on the books in Missouri for a long time before Dobbs, including waiting periods and informed consent. This underscores the truth about abortion activists. They aren’t really “pro-choice,” because that would imply that they would want women to have all the information before making such a monumental decision as a tragic if “necessary” evil. Abortion activists are pro-abortion because they view abortion as a positive good. Indeed, much abortion advocacy adopts pseudosacral language and behavior, which makes sense once we understand it as a sacrifice to the false god of sexual satisfaction.

While the United States is not yet the culture of life that John Paul II called upon the faithful to build, neither is America on the whole a radical culture of death that pro-abortion forces wish it to be. But Americans need to wake up and take notice of the big-money campaign of lies and deception that seeks to metastasize the culture of death one state at a time.

He was the most beautiful of all the angels and the most exalted beneath God. Yet at some point, he determined to be exalted ABOVE God. That’s when the battle began. What was it like—when Lucifer fell? This week on The Land and the Book, we’ll take a biblical look at…“The Battle for Heaven and Earth.”
